title: Don't you want to be forgiven?
hook: Abu Bakr forgives a relative who spread the slander after this verse: pardon and overlook (24:22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, uns, knock and greet, and your line was ask before entering. Which door did you knock on and wait? Day four hundred ninety-six.

Three days ago we heard the rumor about 'A'isha. Now the other side of it. Her father, Abu Bakr, had a poor relative named Mistah, a cousin's son, and for years Abu Bakr had been paying for his keep. When the slander spread, Mistah was one of the people repeating it. About his own benefactor's daughter. After the verses came down clearing her, Abu Bakr swore an oath: he would never spend on Mistah again. Most of us would call that fair. Then another verse came down.

Verse twenty-two. It speaks to people of means who swear not to give to their relatives, the poor, and those who emigrated for God's sake. Mistah was all three. And then, in Pickthall's words: "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" Two verbs again. Ya'fu: to pardon, to let the debt go. Yasfahu: to overlook, to turn away from it, to stop bringing it up. Scholars often describe the second as going one step further than the first: not only letting the wrong go, but not holding it over the person afterward. And then the question. Not a command, a question. Don't you want God to forgive you? 'A'isha's account in Bukhari says that when Abu Bakr heard this, he said: yes, by God, I want God to forgive me. And he went back to supporting Mistah, and said he would never stop. Look at what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say Mistah was right. It doesn't say the harm was small; the verses before called it great. It doesn't ask Abu Bakr to trust Mistah with secrets. It asks him not to cut off the support that kept a poor relative fed. Pardon isn't pretending it didn't happen, and it isn't letting someone keep hurting you. It's refusing to make the rest of the relationship pay for one wound. And the reason it gives is personal. Everyone needs forgiving for something.
screen: `AN OATH TO STOP GIVING.` · `PARDON, AND OVERLOOK.` · `DON'T YOU WANT TO BE FORGIVEN?` · `YES, BY GOD. THE SUPPORT RESUMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pardon someone who hurt you. Start small. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone who hurt you in a modest way: a careless word, a broken promise, a snub. Not the deepest wound, and not anyone who is still harming you. Notice what you've been holding back from them because of it. Then ask yourself the verse's question, gently. If you pray, you can ask to be able to let it go, and to be forgiven too. The bell holds the time.
Mistah. The poor relative who spread the rumor about 'A'isha, and whom Abu Bakr chose to keep supporting anyway. Today's word.
Your line: pardon, and be pardoned. Today, give back one small thing you'd been withholding from someone over an old hurt: a greeting, a reply, a kindness. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often tell the story of Abu Bakr and Mistah with 24:22 when speaking about forgiveness within families, and many Muslims recall its question when they find it hard to let go of a grievance.

myth: the verse says Mistah did nothing wrong
the verses before call the slander great in God's sight. 24:22 asks for pardon anyway.
Abu Bakr resumed supporting Mistah after the verse
he said, yes, by God, I want God to forgive me, and returned to supporting him.
pardon in this verse means trusting the person exactly as before
it asks not to cut off his support. it doesn't ask Abu Bakr to pretend nothing happened.

fork.setup: you're Abu Bakr. you've sworn never to support Mistah again. then you hear: don't you want God to forgive you? what do you do?
options: keep the oath; it was sworn before God.
say yes, by God, and go back to supporting him.
support him, but quietly tell people what he did.
fork.reveal: he said yes, by God, I want God to forgive me, and resumed supporting Mistah, saying he would never stop.

original.note: Arabic: let them pardon and let them overlook, from 24:22.

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to people who wronged you.
what it means: don't cut off the good you were doing because of one wound; pardon, overlook, and remember you need forgiving too.
what a scholar hears: 'afw and safh paired, safh often explained as going beyond 'afw; 'A'isha reports Abu Bakr's response in Bukhari 4750; the verse addresses ulu l-fadl, people of means.

sources.quoted: Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?

notes: Pickthall wording of 24:22 quoted from memory; please confirm exactly.
Mistah's relation to Abu Bakr: commonly given as the son of Abu Bakr's maternal cousin (or his aunt's son); the script says 'a cousin's son'. Confirm.
'Scholars often describe' safh as going further than 'afw (e.g. al-Raghib al-Isfahani); confirm.
The practice deliberately limits pardon to small hurts and excludes anyone still causing harm; confirm this framing is acceptable.
